Each location uses its own point-of-sale system, either Compilator or Eontyre. Customer, order, invoice, and tire storage data is collected from these systems and stored in a central Postgres database. The data is then cleaned and organized into tables and KPI views that cover orders, revenue, tire storage usage, and customer data quality.

customer information, including names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, organization numbers, and license plates, all linked to the relevant shop.

They’re “split” because they come from different teams with different goals and security philosophies. Yes, CalyxOS is strong enough for daily use—but GrapheneOS is objectively stricter and more hardened.
1) Why GrapheneOS and CalyxOS are separate projects
They are not forks of each other in a simple way. They diverged because of
ideology + technical direction
.
GrapheneOS philosophy
Focus:
maximum security + minimal attack surface
Key points:
No Google Play by default (optional sandboxed Play Services)
Strong memory hardening, exploit mitigations, SELinux tuning
Very strict security model
Minimal convenience features if they weaken security
Pixel-only devices (for hardware security reasons)
Think of it as:
“Security first, even if usability suffers.”
CalyxOS philosophy
Focus:
privacy + usability balance
Key points:
MicroG included by default (Google compatibility without Google)
Easier app compatibility
More user-friendly defaults
Less aggressive hardening than GrapheneOS
Supports more devices (not only Pixel)
Think of it as:
“Privacy-friendly Android that normal people can use daily.”

Yes — for most people.
CalyxOS is:
More private than stock Android

Stable enough for daily driver

Hardened malloc / memory allocator

CalyxOS adds:

, date of birth, medical record number, SSN (about ~25-35%), along with multiple other identifiers and detailed PHI, including referral documents and often COMPLETE MEDICAL RECORDS.
Note: There are close to
a million unique patients in the clinical notes
(see below), but we are only counting the 160,000 that can be cross-referenced and identified by name via the data that we possess.
- Clinical Notes:

of doctors and nurses on their patients, documenting the most sensitive medical information imaginable
- S3 EMR Files:

~93,000 clinical wound photographs of an extraordinarily graphic nature
- Insurance Records:
5,181,555 capitation records
spanning patients from newborns to 96-year-olds
- Staff Exposed:

- Production Creds:
Django superuser passwords, database connection strings, Azure AD secrets. Thank you Woundtech, for helping us lateral with ease through your environment!
---
Samples from the clinical notes:
Paul A█████, 39, Male, Blue Shield:
> "History obtained from patient's sister. Patient is a 39 year old male with a history of schizophrenia. Patient has a mobility impairment and spends prolonged periods of time in bed... Barriers to healing: Decreased mobility, incontinence, Schizophrenia, Parkinson. Patient is bed bound, malnutrition (BMI 17.8)."
His full name, DOB (June 28, 1985), Blue Shield subscriber ID, and complete psychiatric history — all cross-referenced in a dataset that was sitting unencrypted on S3.
Fei W███, 63, Male, Anthem Blue Cross:
> "S - Wound on right dorsal foot. Reports that he has injected heroin once since previous visit. Patient is in excruciating pain from self-removing the old dressing. A - Wound type - heroin injection usage"
And from another note on the same patient:
> "Patient has history of injecting himself with heroin and is the reason he developed abscess wounds."
His Anthem Blue Cross subscriber information, his SSN (in his medical record PDF), his doctor's name — linked directly to documentation of his heroin use.
Christina M█████, 25, Female, United Healthcare:
> "Social Hx: Methamphetamine abuse, daily smoker, alcohol abuse. Barriers to healing: Insulin dependent DM2, DM polyneuropathy, history of recurring and current Methamphetamine use, non compliant with follow up with multiple no shows and cancelled appointments."
She's barely 25 years old, and her complete substance abuse history is stored alongside her United Healthcare subscriber ID.
Lawrence H██████, 66, Male, Blue Shield:
> "Barriers to healing: HTN, HLD, ESRD, paraplegia, HIV, lack of social support, substance abuse, poor nutrition"
His HIV status. His full name. His DOB (March 24, 1959). His Blue Shield insurance. All connected. All exposed.
---
When these patients spoke to their healthcare providers about their most personal and private issues and experiences, do you think they expected these confessions to be stored so insecurely a rudimentary hack would allow access to them? Would they have allowed wound care nurses to photograph their heroin injection wounds, bedsore ulcers and diabetic foot wounds?
They never imagined these documents and images would end up in S3 buckets configured with credentials sitting in unencrypted Terraform state files.
Shame on you, Woundtech, for breaking that trust so cavalierly.
---
A note on redactions:
To avoid re-victimizing the patients that Woundtech has already betrayed, we've redacted surnames and partially redacted patient phone numbers, SSNs, addresses, MRNs, and some other identifying data. We are in the process of partially redacting the entire data set to maintain patient privacy while still fully documenting the breach.
We do this because these patients did nothing wrong. They developed wounds that required professional care. They trusted their healthcare providers to protect their most intimate information. Woundtech doubly betrayed that trust, first when they prioritized speed-to-market over basic security hygiene, and now Woundtech has let them down yet again by refusing to pay a modest fee to protect their private data.
We look forward to watching the upcoming class action lawsuits against this terrible company.
